\textbf{Current.}
Fix $e_{\beta},e_{\alpha}\in\R^2$, with $e_{\beta}$ the field direction
and $e_{\alpha}$ the current direction.
For all $\varepsilon\geq0$ and $t\geq0$, define
\begin{gather*}
  \gamma_0=\ind_{(-\infty,\mu_{\mathrm F}]}(H),
  \qquad H_\varepsilon=H-\varepsilon x\cdot e_{\beta},
  \qquad J_{\alpha}=(-i\nabla)\cdot e_{\alpha},\\
  \gamma_\varepsilon(t)
  =e^{-itH_\varepsilon}\gamma_0e^{itH_\varepsilon},
  \qquad
  j_\varepsilon(t)
  =\trv\bigl(J_{\alpha}\gamma_\varepsilon(t)\bigr),
\end{gather*}
where $H_\varepsilon$ denotes the self-adjoint closure of its
restriction to $C_c^\infty(\R^2;\C)$, and
\[
  \trv(A)=\frac1{|\Omega|}\Tr(\ind_\Omega A\ind_\Omega)
\]
for locally trace-class periodic $A$.

\begin{theorem}
Under the above assumptions, the iterated limit exists and
\[
\lim_{T\to+\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T
  \left(\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}
  \frac{j_\varepsilon(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)\,dt
  =\frac{M}{16}\,e_{\alpha}\cdot e_{\beta}.
\]
\end{theorem}

Dominated convergence in \eqref{eq:scaled-integral} therefore yields

 =\cB\int_{S^1}\frac{f_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)}{4v_i}\,d\omega

\end{equation}
The scalar integral is $\pi v_i$. One self-contained evaluation starts
from $u^{-2}=\int_0^\infty y e^{-yu}\,dy$: by Tonelli,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-integral}
 \int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}\,du
 =\int_0^\infty y\left(\frac1y-\frac{y}{1+y^2}\right)dy
 =\frac\pi2.
\end{equation}
Using \eqref{eq:angular-integral} in \eqref{eq:cone-limit-integral}, we
obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:one-cone}
 \lim_{T\to\infty}I_i(T)
 =\frac1{(2\pi)^2}\,\frac\pi4\,

 =\frac1{16}\,e_\alpha\cdot e_\beta.
\end{equation}
Summing over the $M$ crossings and adding the vanishing contribution
from the other transitions proves \cref{thm:main}.

The calculation also explains the independence from $v_i$: the two
current matrix elements supply a factor $v_i^2$, while the radial gap
and its integration supply the inverse factor. Ces\`aro averaging is

*** Add File: review_cones.md
+# Independent review: conical reduction and the universal constant
+
+The theorem in `graphene_statement.tex` is consistent. In particular, its
+eigenvalue assumptions do imply the leading interband matrix elements needed
+for the coefficient \(M/16\); a separate hypothesis on Bloch eigenvectors is
+not needed. The real-valuedness of \(V\) is useful for the exact cancellation
+of the imaginary, antisymmetric response. No online sources were used.
+
+## 1. An analytic two-band frame
+
+Fix one node, put \(q=k-k_i\), \(r=|q|\), and write \(v=v_i\). A fixed contour
+around \(\mu_{\mathrm F}\), enclosing only the double eigenvalue at \(q=0\),
+defines the analytic rank-two Riesz projection \(Q(q)\) for all small \(q\).
+Analyticity holds as an operator into \(H^2_{m per}\), since the fibers have
+a common domain and depend polynomially on \(q\). Choose an isometry
+\(U_0:\mathbb C^2\to\operatorname{Ran}Q(0)\), and set
+
+\[
+ U(q)=Q(q)U_0\bigl(U_0^*Q(q)U_0\bigr)^{-1/2}.
+\]
+
+The inverse square root exists near zero and is real analytic. Thus \(U(q)\)
+is an analytic orthonormal frame for \(\operatorname{Ran}Q(q)\), with values
+in \(H^2_{m per}\). Its reduced Hamiltonian is the Hermitian matrix
+
+\[
+ h(q)=U(q)^*H_{k_i+q}U(q)=a(q)I+d(q)\cdot\sigma,
+ \qquad d(q)\in\mathbb R^3.
+\]
+
+Its eigenvalues are \(a(q)\pm|d(q)|\). The hypotheses imply
+
+\[
+ a(q)=\mu_{\mathrm F}+O(r^2),\qquad
+ d(q)=Lq+O(r^2),\qquad L^*L=v^2I_{\mathbb R^2}.
+\]
+
+Indeed, the first assertion follows by adding the two eigenvalue
+expansions. Analyticity gives \(d=Lq+O(r^2)\); comparison along each ray
+with \(|d(q)|=vr+O(r^2)\) gives \(|L\omega|=v\) for every unit \(\omega\).
+This is exactly \(L^*L=v^2I\). Derivative estimates for the remainders now
+follow from analyticity, without differentiating the original \(O(r^2)\)
+eigenvalue statement.
+
+## 2. The physical velocities
+
+For a direction \(e\), write
+
+\[
+ B_e(q)=U(q)^*(\partial_eH_{k_i+q})U(q),\qquad
+ A_e(q)=U(q)^*\partial_eU(q).
+\]
+
+Differentiation of \(h=U^*HU\), using \(HU=Uh\), gives
+
+\[
+ \partial_e h=B_e+[h,A_e],\qquad
+ B_e(q)=(Le)\cdot\sigma+O(r).
+\]
+
+The connection term is \(O(r)\) because \(h(0)=\mu_{\mathrm F}I\).
+This small term must be mentioned: physical velocities are not literally
+derivatives of the reduced matrix in a moving frame.
+
+Let \(n(q)=d(q)/|d(q)|\), and \(\pi_\pm(q)=(I\pm n(q)\cdot\sigma)/2\).
+The active pair of physical spectral projectors is \(P_\pm=U\pi_\pm U^*\).
+Define
+
+\[
+ z_{\alpha\beta}(q)
+   =\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(P_-(q)(\partial_\alpha H)
+       P_+(q)(\partial_\beta H)\bigr)
+   =\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C^2}
+       \bigl(\pi_-B_\alpha\pi_+B_\beta\bigr).
+\]
+
+The Pauli identity, for \(a,b,n\in\mathbb R^3\) with \(|n|=1\), is
+
+\[
+ \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\pi_-(a\cdot\sigma)
+             \pi_+(b\cdot\sigma)\bigr)
+ =a\cdot b-(a\cdot n)(b\cdot n)-i\,n\cdot(a\times b).
+\]
+
+Consequently, uniformly for \(q=r\omega\),
+
+\[
+ \begin{split}
+ \operatorname{Re}z_{\alpha\beta}(r\omega)
+ &=v^2f_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)+O(r),\\
+ \operatorname{Im}z_{\alpha\beta}(r\omega)&=O(r),\\
+ f_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)
+ &=e_\alpha\cdot e_\beta
+       -(e_\alpha\cdot\omega)(e_\beta\cdot\omega).
+ \end{split}
+\]
+
+The leading imaginary part vanishes because \(L\omega,Le_\alpha,Le_ eta\)
+all belong to the same two-dimensional plane in \(\mathbb R^3\).
+In particular,
+
+\[
+ \int_0^{2\pi}f_{\alpha\beta}(\omega(\theta))\,d\theta
+   =\pi e_\alpha\cdot e_\beta.
+\]
+
+## 3. Exact change to the gap coordinate
+
+Set \(\Delta(q)=\lambda_{N+1}(k_i+q)-\lambda_N(k_i+q)=2|d(q)|\).
+For small fixed \(\delta>0\),
+
+\[
+ \Delta(r\omega)=2vr+O(r^2),\qquad
+ \partial_r\Delta(r\omega)=2v+O(r)>v.
+\]
+
+To justify the derivative uniformly, write
+\(d(r\omega)/r=L\omega+rD(r,\omega)\). This is smooth down to \(r=0\)
+and has norm bounded away from zero. Hence the gap is smooth in \((r,\omega)\)
+up to \(r=0\) and strictly increasing in \(r\).
+
+Use the exact variable \(ho=\Delta(r\omega)\). Its inverse satisfies
+
+\[
+ r=\frac{\rho}{2v}+O(\rho^2),\qquad
+ r\,\partial_\rho r=\frac{\rho}{4v^2}+O(\rho^2).
+\]
+
+For the Cesaro response of this pair,
+
+\[
+ I_T=\frac1{(2\pi)^2}\int_{|q|<\delta}
+ \frac{2\operatorname{Re}z_{\alpha\beta}(q)}{T\Delta(q)^3}
+ \bigl(1-\cos(T\Delta(q))\bigr)\,dq,
+\]
+
+the transformed amplitude is therefore
+
+\[
+ \frac{2\operatorname{Re}z_{\alpha\beta}(r\omega)
+                 r\partial_\rho r}{\rho^3}
+ =\frac{f_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)}{2\rho^2}
+       +O(\rho^{-1}).
+\]
+
+The variable upper limit \(ho_\delta(\omega)=\Delta(\delta\omega)\)
+is bounded above and below by positive constants. The remainder has the
+uniform estimate
+
+\[
+ \frac1T\int_0^{\rho_\delta(\omega)}
+       \frac{1-\cos(T\rho)}\rho\,d\rho
+ =O\!\left(\frac{1+\log T}{T}\right).
+\]
+
+Extending the leading integral from its upper limit to infinity costs
+\(O(T^{-1})\). Since
+
+\[
+ \int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos s}{s^2}\,ds=\frac\pi2,
+\]
+
+we obtain
+
+\[
+ I_T=\frac1{(2\pi)^2}\frac\pi4
+          \int_0^{2\pi}f_{\alpha\beta}(\omega(\theta))\,d\theta
+       +O\!\left(\frac{1+\log T}{T}\right)
+ =\frac1{16}e_\alpha\cdot e_\beta
+       +O\!\left(\frac{1+\log T}{T}\right).
+\]
+
+A short self-contained proof of the scalar integral uses
+\(s^{-2}=\int_0^\infty y e^{-ys}\,dy\). Tonelli, applied to the nonnegative
+integrand, gives
+
+\[
+ \int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos s}{s^2}\,ds
+ =\int_0^\infty y\left(\frac1y-\frac{y}{y^2+1}\right)\,dy
+ =\int_0^\infty\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=\frac\pi2.
+\]
+
+This exact gap substitution avoids uncontrolled replacement of the phase
+\(T\Delta(q)\) by \(2vTr\). Such a replacement is not justified by merely
+writing \(\Delta=2vr+O(r^2)\) when \(T\to\infty\).
+
+## 4. Other transitions and the antisymmetric part
+
+Outside the active pair in sufficiently small node disks, all occupied to
+unoccupied gaps have a uniform positive lower bound. The sum over all
+unoccupied states is absolutely controlled by
+
+\[
+ \sum_{n\le N,m>N}|z_{nm}^{\alpha\beta}(k)|
+ \le\left(\sum_{n\le N}\|v_\alpha(k)u_n(k)\|^2\right)^{1/2}
+      \left(\sum_{n\le N}\|v_\beta(k)u_n(k)\|^2\right)^{1/2}.
+\]
+
+The right side is uniformly finite on a compact Brillouin zone. Therefore
+their symmetric Cesaro contribution is \(O(T^{-1})\), and no stationary
+phase theorem, regularity of remote bands, or absence of critical energies
+is required.
+
+If the linear response formula also contains imaginary terms, use the
+exact real-\(V\) time-reversal identity. Complex conjugation maps \(H_k\) to
+\(H_{-k}\) and \(v_\alpha(k)\) to \(-v_\alpha(-k)\); thus transition gaps
+are even and the corresponding summed imaginary matrix elements are odd.
+Their Brillouin-zone integrals vanish. The active-pair static quantity
+\(\operatorname{Im}z/\Delta^2=O(1/r)\) is locally integrable, so even a
+formula separated into its static and oscillatory imaginary terms remains
+legitimate. For finite time, cancellation can instead be invoked before
+that separation, with the bounded cosine kernel.
+
+## 5. Useful regularity for the Drude cancellation
+
+Let \(E(k)=\sum_{n\le N}\lambda_n(k)\), defined continuously at the nodes.
+Near the chosen node it has the form
+
+\[
+ E(k_i+q)=S(q)+a(q)-|d(q)|,
+\]
+
+where \(S\) is the analytic trace of \(H\) on the lower, rank-\(N-1\)
+cluster. Consequently \(
abla E=O(1)\) and \(D^2E=O(1/r)\) away from the
+node. In particular \(E\in W^{2,1}\) on the Brillouin torus, and there is
+no point-mass term in its distributional Hessian. One can prove the latter
+directly by deleting disks of radius \(\eta\): the boundary term involving
+\(
abla E\) is \(O(\eta)\), hence vanishes. Thus
+
+\[
+ \int_{\mathcal B}\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta E(k)\,dk=0.
+\]
+
+On the punctured torus the second derivative identity is
+
+\[
+ \partial_\alpha\partial_\beta E
+ =N e_\alpha\cdot e_\beta
+   -2\sum_{n\le N,m>N}
+        \frac{\operatorname{Re}z_{nm}^{\alpha\beta}}
+             {\lambda_m-\lambda_n}.
+\]
+
